title: Finding food and staying alive: how animals hunt, graze and hide

summary.text: Every animal, including us, has two jobs each day: find food, and not become someone else's food. Searching for food and getting it is called foraging. Plant eaters such as cows and elephants graze or browse for most of the day, because grass and leaves give little energy in each mouthful. Hunters chase their prey, wait in ambush, or build traps, and most of their hunts fail. Prey animals stay alive by watching, keeping still, running, living in groups and hiding. Hiding by matching the place where you rest is called camouflage, and it works only while the body and the place match.
summary.art: A sunny Indian forest meadow: a herd of spotted deer grazing under a tree full of grey langur monkeys, a tiger lying low in golden grass at the edge, and a brown nightjar sitting on dry leaves in the foreground.

intro.hook: Cut 20 small strips from a newspaper and 20 from plain paper. Scatter them all over an open newspaper on the floor. Now pick up as many as you can in 20 seconds, one at a time. Which ones did you miss?
intro.text: Picking small strips off a newspaper is like what a bird does every day when she hunts insects on a tree. The insects stay alive only if the bird misses them. In this unit you find out how animals find their food: by grazing, browsing, chasing, waiting and trapping. You also find out how prey animals stay alive, and why a body that is hidden in one place can be easy to see in another.
intro.art: A child kneeling over a newspaper spread on a floor, quickly picking up small white paper strips, while strips cut from newspaper lie unnoticed all around her hand.

outcomes: I can explain what foraging means, and name ways animals get food: grazing, browsing, hunting, scavenging and filtering.
I can describe three ways predators hunt, which are chasing, waiting in ambush and setting a trap, with an Indian animal for each.
I can explain why plant eaters such as cows and elephants spend most of the day eating.
I can run a fair test with paper prey, and use my results to explain how camouflage works and why it depends on the background.
I can name ways prey animals stay alive: watching, keeping still, running, living in groups, alarm calls, shells and spines.
I can explain that hunters and their prey have shaped each other over a very long time, and say what scientists still do not know.

terms.meaning: To forage is to search for food and get it, by finding, collecting or catching it. Every animal forages in their own way.
terms.example: A myna walking across a lawn and pecking at insects in the grass is foraging.
terms.art: A myna bird walking on short grass with an insect in her yellow beak.

terms.meaning: A predator is an animal who hunts and eats other animals.
terms.example: A pond heron standing in a paddy field is a predator of small fish and frogs.
terms.art: A brown pond heron standing in shallow water in a paddy field, neck pulled in, watching the water.

terms.meaning: Prey are the animals that a predator hunts and eats.
terms.example: Moths and mosquitoes are prey for the house gecko on your wall.
terms.art: A house gecko on a wall beside a tube light, a moth fluttering close by.

terms.meaning: A herbivore is an animal who eats only plants.
terms.example: Cows, goats, elephants and spotted deer are herbivores.
terms.art: A cow, a goat and an elephant, each eating a different plant.

terms.meaning: A carnivore is an animal who eats mainly other animals.
terms.example: Tigers, spiders, frogs and kingfishers are carnivores.
terms.art: A kingfisher on a wire with a small silver fish in her beak.

terms.meaning: An omnivore is an animal who eats both plants and animals.
terms.example: Crows eat grain, fruit, insects and leftovers. Most humans are omnivores too.
terms.art: A crow on a wall pecking at a bowl with rice, a piece of banana and a beetle beside it.

terms.meaning: A scavenger eats animals that are already dead, or food that others have left behind.
terms.example: Vultures and crows are scavengers. They clear away dead animals.
terms.art: Three vultures standing around a dead animal in a dry field.

terms.meaning: To graze is to eat grass or other low plants, bite after bite, while moving slowly along.
terms.example: Buffaloes eating grass on the bank of a canal near Thanjavur are grazing.
terms.art: Two water buffaloes with their heads down, grazing on a green canal bank.

terms.meaning: To browse is to eat leaves, shoots and twigs from bushes and trees.
terms.example: A goat standing on her back legs to reach the leaves of a bush is browsing.
terms.art: A goat standing on her back legs, front hooves on a branch, nibbling leaves.

terms.meaning: An ambush is a hunt in which the predator waits, still and hidden, and attacks when the prey comes close.
terms.example: A mugger crocodile lying still in a river, with only her eyes above the water, is waiting in ambush.
terms.art: Two crocodile eyes and a nose just above the surface of a brown river, a deer drinking at the bank.

terms.meaning: Camouflage is colour, pattern or shape that makes a body hard to see against the place where they are.
terms.example: An oakleaf butterfly with her wings closed looks just like a dry brown leaf.
terms.art: An oakleaf butterfly with closed wings among real dry leaves on a twig, hard to tell apart.

terms.meaning: Countershading means being darker on the back and paler on the belly. Light from above brightens the back and leaves the belly in shadow. The dark back and pale belly even this out, so the body looks flat and is harder to see.
terms.example: A mackerel, called bangda in many Indian markets, is dark blue on top and silvery white underneath.
terms.art: A mackerel fish seen from the side, dark blue-green back and silver-white belly.

terms.meaning: An alarm call is a sound an animal makes when they spot danger. Others who hear it look up, run or hide.
terms.example: When crows spot a cat, they caw loudly again and again, and more crows fly in.
terms.art: Several crows on a wall cawing with beaks open, a cat below looking up at them.

terms.meaning: A herd is a big group of animals, such as deer or cattle, who feed and move together. A group of birds is a flock, and a group of fish is a school.
terms.example: Spotted deer, called chital, graze in herds in Bandipur and Kanha.
terms.art: A herd of spotted deer grazing in a meadow, two of them with heads raised, looking around.

terms.meaning: Cows, buffaloes, goats and deer swallow their food quickly, then later bring it back up into the mouth and chew it again. This is called chewing the cud.
terms.example: A cow lying on the road, chewing slowly with no food in front of her, is chewing the cud.
terms.art: A cow lying down on a quiet street, eyes half closed, jaw moving.

explanations.definition: Foraging is searching for food and getting it: finding it, catching or collecting it, and eating it.
explanations.description: Every animal forages, from an ant to an elephant. Humans are animals, and we forage too. For most of human history, people gathered fruit, seeds and roots, fished and hunted. Many people still pick wild greens, fish and collect honey. Foraging always costs something. It takes time and energy, and it can be dangerous, because a hungry animal out in the open may be seen by a predator. So every forager balances two needs: eat enough, and stay safe.
examples: A purple sunbird visits flower after flower, drinking nectar with a long, curved beak.
Flamingos in the Rann of Kutch dip their heads upside down in shallow water and strain out tiny animals and plants with their beaks.
In the Nilgiris, Kurumba honey gatherers climb cliffs to collect honey from the nests of wild rock bees.
explanations.art: A wheel of foragers: a sunbird at a flower, a flamingo with her head upside down in water, a goat at a bush, a gecko at a tube light, and a woman gathering greens.
explanations.context: This card says what foraging means. Every animal, including you, forages every day.

explanations.concept: Grazers and browsers eat for most of the day
explanations.definition: Herbivores who eat grass are called grazers. Herbivores who eat the leaves and twigs of bushes and trees are called browsers.
explanations.description: Grass and leaves are easy to find, but each mouthful gives little energy. They are also tough and slow to digest. So a plant eater must eat a lot, and spend much of the day eating. Cows, buffaloes, goats and deer have a stomach with four parts. Tiny living things called microbes live in it and help break down the tough plants. These animals swallow quickly while feeding. Later, while resting, they chew the cud, which grinds the food finer. Every moment spent with the head down to eat is a moment the animal cannot watch for danger. That is one reason grazers feed in herds.
examples: An adult Asian elephant feeds for most of the day and part of the night, and can eat well over 100 kilograms of plants in a day.
A goat browses on a thorny bush, picking the leaves out between the thorns with her lips.
Chital deer often feed under trees where grey langur monkeys are eating, and pick up the leaves and fruit the langurs drop.
explanations.art: An elephant pulling a bunch of grass with her trunk, and a sun moving across the sky above her from morning to night.
explanations.context: This card explains why plant eaters such as cows and elephants spend so much of the day eating.

explanations.concept: Three ways to hunt: chase, ambush and trap
explanations.definition: A predator who chases runs, flies or swims after prey. A predator in ambush waits, still and hidden, until prey comes close. A predator with a trap builds something that catches prey for them.
explanations.description: Chasing uses a lot of energy, so chasers usually hunt in short bursts, or hunt together. Dholes, India's wild dogs, hunt in packs and chase deer for a long way. Ambush hunters save energy by waiting. A pond heron stands still in shallow water, then stabs at a fish. A tiger creeps close through tall grass, keeping low, and then rushes. Trappers build. A spider spins a sticky web and waits. An antlion larva, the young of a winged insect, digs a cone-shaped pit in dry dust and waits at the bottom for an ant to slip in. Most hunts fail. A tiger often has to try many times before she makes a kill.
examples: A house gecko waits beside a tube light, where moths and flies gather, then darts.
Dragonflies catch other insects in the air. In one study, some dragonflies caught their prey in more than 9 out of every 10 tries.
Banded archerfish in the mangroves of the Sundarbans spit a jet of water to knock insects off leaves into the water.
explanations.art: Three small pictures side by side: a pack of dholes running after a deer; a tiger crouched low in grass; a spider waiting in the middle of a web.
explanations.context: This card is about how predators catch their food. There are three main ways.

explanations.concept: Scavengers and omnivores eat what they find
explanations.definition: A scavenger eats animals that are already dead, or food others leave. An omnivore eats both plants and animals.
explanations.description: Not every meat eater hunts. Vultures can spot a dead animal from high in the sky and clear the body away within hours. This stops the dead body rotting and spreading disease. Crows are both omnivores and scavengers. They eat grain, fruit, insects, eggs and leftovers. Because they eat so many kinds of food, crows do well almost anywhere, including in big cities. Humans are omnivores too.
examples: A crow carries a piece of chapati to a water tank and dips it to soften it.
Kites circle over fish markets in Chennai and Kolkata, swooping down for scraps.
Jackals eat fruit, insects and the leftovers of other hunters' kills.
explanations.art: A kite swooping low over a busy fish market, a crow on the roof edge watching.
explanations.context: This card is about animals who eat what they find, instead of hunting or grazing.

explanations.concept: Camouflage: a match between a body and a place
explanations.definition: Camouflage is colour, pattern or shape that makes a body hard to see in the place where they are.
explanations.description: Camouflage works only against the right background. A green leaf insect is hidden among green leaves, but easy to see on a white wall. The Paper Caterpillars experiment shows the same thing: newspaper strips are hard to find on a newspaper, but easy to find on a plain sheet. Many camouflaged animals also choose where to rest. Some moths land on bark, then walk and turn until their pattern lines up with the cracks in the bark. A team of scientists in South Korea filmed this in 2012. Stripes and spots break up the outline of a body, so a hunter's eye cannot easily find the edge. Countershading, a dark back and a pale belly, evens out the shadow under the body.
examples: Oakleaf butterflies in India's forests look like a dry leaf when their wings are closed, with a line like the middle vein of a leaf.
Ghost crabs on the beaches of Chennai and Puri are the colour of sand, and dash into their burrows when something comes near.
A jungle nightjar lays her eggs on bare ground and sits on them all day, her streaky brown feathers matching the dead leaves around her.
explanations.art: A grey moth on a tree trunk, half-hidden, next to the same moth on a white wall, where she is easy to see.
explanations.context: This card explains camouflage, which you test in the Paper Caterpillars experiment. Hiding depends on the place as well as the body.

explanations.concept: What does a deer see when a tiger is near?
explanations.description: To us, a tiger is bright orange. But deer have eyes that see fewer colours than ours do. Scientists who studied deer eyes think that, to a deer, orange looks much like green. If they are right, a tiger in green grass is better hidden from a deer than from us. So camouflage depends on three things together: the body, the place, and the eyes that look. Many birds can also see ultraviolet light, which human eyes cannot see at all. A pattern that looks plain to us might stand out to a bird.
examples: Bees see ultraviolet patterns on flowers that we cannot see.
A tiger's orange coat may look green to a deer in tall grass, but bright to a person in a jeep.
explanations.art: The same tiger in grass drawn twice: on the left in bright orange as people see her, on the right in dull greens as a deer might see her.
explanations.context: This card asks whether other animals see a hunter the way we do. Scientists have ideas, but nobody can look through a deer's eyes.

explanations.concept: Staying alive: watch, keep still, run and stay together
explanations.definition: Prey animals stay alive by noticing danger early, keeping still, running away, living in groups, and carrying protection such as shells or spines.
explanations.description: Many hunters notice movement first. So a prey animal who keeps still is harder to spot. The Still or Moving experiment shows this: a wriggling paper strip is spotted much sooner than a still one. Living in a group helps too. A herd or flock has many eyes, so someone spots the predator sooner, and each animal can spend more time eating. An alarm call warns everyone. Chital deer and langur monkeys listen to each other's alarm calls. Langurs sitting high in trees can see a tiger or leopard from far away, and chital have a sharp sense of smell. Some animals carry protection. A tortoise pulls into her shell, an Indian pangolin rolls into a ball of hard scales, and a porcupine raises and rattles sharp quills.
examples: In a study in England, a trained hawk caught fewer pigeons from big flocks than from small ones, because big flocks noticed the hawk and flew off sooner.
A chital who senses danger stamps a front foot, gives a sharp alarm call and raises her tail to show its white underside.
A frog in a pond freezes and stays very still when a heron's shadow passes.
explanations.art: A flock of pigeons bursting up from a road all at once, a hawk shape high above them.
explanations.context: This card is about how prey animals stay alive. Hiding is only one of their ways.

explanations.concept: Hunters and prey shape each other
explanations.definition: Over a very long time, predators and prey change together. When prey get better at hiding or escaping, the predators who survive are the ones better at finding and catching them. Scientists sometimes call this an arms race.
explanations.description: This happens over many, many generations, not in one animal's life. Prey who were easy to see were eaten more often, so fewer of them had young. Over thousands of generations, the colours that stay hidden became common. Hunters who could not find enough prey also had fewer young. A deer's sharp ears and fast legs, and a tiger's stripes and quiet paws, make sense only together. Hunting is very old. The family of jellyfish, corals and sea anemones is the oldest group of animals known to hunt with venom. Their tentacles carry stinging cells that fire like tiny harpoons.
examples: Bats hunt moths by listening for echoes. Some moths can hear a bat's calls and drop to the ground or fly in loops to escape.
A tiger's soft paw pads let her walk almost silently, and a deer's large ears can turn to catch tiny sounds.
explanations.art: A long ribbon of time showing a tiger and a deer changing side by side over many generations, each one turned towards the other.
explanations.context: This card explains how hunters and prey change each other, very slowly, over many generations.

explanations.concept: Do animals think and feel while they hunt and hide?
explanations.description: Hunters and prey make decisions all the time: where to look, when to strike, when to give up, where to rest. A spider who catches little often moves her web somewhere else. A moth turns on the bark until she is hidden. A tiger who has been seen walks away instead of wasting a chase. These are choices made by thinking, feeling beings. Some scientists call much of this automatic behaviour, shaped over many generations. Scientists still argue about what each animal feels.
examples: A house gecko picks the spot beside the tube light, where insects gather, and comes back to it night after night.
A chital who hears a langur's alarm call stops eating and looks towards the danger.

perspectives.explanation: Hunting and hiding are full of choices that change with the situation. Prey animals show fear in their bodies the way we do: their hearts race, and they freeze or run. It makes sense to say they think and feel.
Much of hunting and hiding is behaviour an animal is born with, shaped over many generations. We should be careful not to assume an animal feels exactly what a human would feel in the same place.

explanations.art: A tiger lying in grass with a thought bubble showing a herd of deer, and a deer with raised head and a thought bubble showing the tall grass.
explanations.context: This card asks what goes on inside a hunter and a hunted animal. Scientists do not all agree.

agreed.text: Every animal must find food, and most must also avoid being eaten. Different animals do this in very different ways.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have watched how thousands of kinds of animals feed, in the wild and in zoos.

In experiments, wild birds were given paper or pastry 'insects' of different colours. They ate fewer of the ones that matched the background. The Paper Caterpillars experiment shows the same thing with paper strips on a newspaper.

agreed.text: Grass and leaves give less energy in each mouthful than meat does, so plant eaters spend more of their day eating.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have timed how long animals feed, and measured the energy in their food.

agreed.text: Living in a group helps prey notice predators sooner.
agreed.evidence: In a study in England, a trained hawk caught fewer pigeons from big flocks than from small ones. Studies of many birds and deer found that animals in bigger groups each look up less, yet the group notices danger sooner.

agreed.text: Most hunts by tigers and lions end without a kill.
agreed.evidence: People who have watched tigers and lions for years have counted many more failed hunts than successful ones.

challenging.claim: A tiger can catch any animal she chooses.
challenging.for: Tigers are big, strong and fast, and they are top predators in Indian forests.
challenging.against: Most of a tiger's hunts fail. Deer hear, smell or see her, and run. Once she has been seen, she usually gives up. A tiger may go several days without a kill.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that big hunters always win.

challenging.who: A common idea, from films that show only the kills
challenging.for: Films and photos usually show the moment a hunter catches someone.
challenging.against: Prey animals escape most attacks. They keep watch, give alarm calls, run, kick, hide, and live in groups. Films show the kills because they are rare and dramatic.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that prey animals cannot defend themselves.

challenging.claim: Chameleons change colour mainly to hide.
challenging.for: A resting chameleon's greens and browns do help them hide among leaves.
challenging.against: Studies by Devi Stuart-Fox, a scientist in Australia, and her colleagues suggest that chameleons change colour most when signalling to other chameleons, for example in a contest or when courting. Temperature matters too.
challenging.context: This card is about why chameleons change colour. The answer surprised many people.

challenging.claim: Every colour on every animal is there to hide them.
challenging.who: Abbott Thayer, an American painter, in a book of 1909
challenging.for: Many animals really are hidden by their colours. Thayer was right about countershading.
challenging.against: Some colours are for showing off, such as a peacock's tail, or for warning that an animal tastes bad. A pink flamingo is not hidden against the sunset.
challenging.context: This card is about a man who was right about one kind of camouflage, then went too far.

challenging.for: Chimpanzees eat mostly fruit and leaves.
challenging.against: In 1960, Jane Goodall saw wild chimpanzees in Gombe, Tanzania, eating meat. Later she saw them hunt monkeys together. Our closest cousins are omnivores, like most humans.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake scientists made about our closest animal cousins.

big_questions.q: In the Paper Caterpillars experiment, the newspaper strips were hard to find on the newspaper, but easy to see on the plain sheet. Is being hidden something the strip has, or something that happens between the strip and the place?
big_questions.hint: Did anything about the strip change when it moved from the newspaper to the plain sheet?

big_questions.q: A deer may see a tiger's orange coat as green. Which is the real colour of the tiger: the one we see, or the one the deer sees?
big_questions.hint: Is colour in the tiger's fur, in the light, or in the eyes? Could it be in all three together?

big_questions.q: Why does keeping still make an animal so much harder to see?
big_questions.hint: Think of the Still or Moving experiment, where one paper strip kept still and one wriggled. Which did your eyes notice first?

big_questions.q: Every eater is also food for someone. When a tiger dies, her body feeds vultures, beetles and the soil. Is anyone only an eater and never food?
big_questions.hint: The soil feeds the grass, and the grass feeds the deer. Who does the deer feed? And who feeds the soil?

big_questions.q: Is it wrong for a tiger to hunt a deer? Is it wrong to feel sad for the deer?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens to the tiger's cubs if she never catches anything.

big_questions.q: Humans are animals. How do people forage in a city? Is a market a kind of forest?
big_questions.hint: Think of how your family finds food, chooses it, and stays safe while doing it.

story.title: The Bird on the Jeep Track
story.note: Bandipur Tiger Reserve in Karnataka, chital, grey langurs, jungle nightjars, house geckos and the way chital and langurs listen to each other's alarm calls are all real. Meenakshi, Arun, Lakshmi and this morning are made up.
text: Meenakshi had waited all year for this summer. Her aunt, Lakshmi Chikkamma, was a forest watcher in Bandipur, in Karnataka. This summer, Meenakshi and her cousin Arun were allowed to ride with her on the morning round.

Arun was eleven. He had watched a hundred wildlife films on his tablet in Bengaluru, and he told everyone so. 'I know everything about tigers,' he said, as the jeep bumped along the red mud track. 'They are the best hunters in the world. They catch whatever they want.'
Lakshmi Chikkamma smiled and said nothing. She stopped the jeep, pointed at the track just ahead of the front wheel, and whispered, 'Tell me what you see.'
Arun looked. 'Dry leaves. Mud. Some stones.'
Meenakshi looked for a long time. One of the dry leaves had an eye. The eye blinked. 'A bird!' she whispered. 'Sitting right on the ground!'

It was a nightjar. Her feathers were brown, grey and black, in tiny streaks and spots, just like the dead leaves around her. 'She is sitting on her eggs,' said Lakshmi Chikkamma. 'Nightjars make no nest. They lay their eggs on bare ground. All day she sits still, and her feathers hide her. At dusk she flies up to catch moths.' She steered the jeep carefully around the bird, who did not move a single feather.
'How did you see her?' Arun asked, a little cross.
'I looked for something that did not belong,' said Meenakshi. 'Her eye was shiny. Leaves are not shiny.'

Further on, the track opened into a grassy meadow near a waterhole. A herd of chital, the spotted deer, was grazing. Above them, in a big tree, a troop of grey langur monkeys sat eating leaves. Every now and then a langur dropped a leafy twig, and a deer nibbled it up.
'Why do the deer stand under the monkeys?' Meenakshi asked.

'Watch how they eat,' said Lakshmi Chikkamma. 'Each deer takes a bite, chews, and lifts their head to look and listen. Then they bite again. Grass gives so little energy that they must eat for most of the day. But while a deer's head is down, they cannot see. So they eat together, and many eyes keep watch. The langurs sit high up, where they can see far. And the leaves they drop are a gift.'
Arun was counting. 'Twenty-two deer. Twenty-two times two is forty-four eyes. And the monkeys have more.'
Suddenly a langur gave a loud, harsh bark. Then another. Every chital lifted their head at once. One stamped a front foot. A deer gave a high, sharp call, and white tails went up all over the herd.
'Alarm calls,' whispered Lakshmi Chikkamma. 'The langurs have seen something. Now the deer are telling everyone, even the hunter, that they have seen her.' She switched off the engine. Nobody spoke.
Arun stared at the tall golden grass at the edge of the meadow. 'There's nothing there,' he whispered.

Meenakshi stared too. She tried her trick. What did not belong? Then she saw it. Two black stripes curved a little differently from the shadows of the grass stems. A round ear, with a white spot on the back, gave a flick. 'Tiger,' she breathed.

The tiger was lying flat, perhaps forty steps from the nearest deer. Her orange and black coat melted into the dry grass and the stripes of shadow between the stems. She must have been creeping closer for a long time. Now every deer was looking straight at her.
The tiger lifted her head and looked at the herd. The herd looked back. For a long moment, nothing moved. Then the tiger stood up, stretched, and walked slowly away into the trees.
Arun let out his breath. 'She didn't even try! I thought tigers caught whatever they wanted.'

'Most of a tiger's hunts fail,' said Lakshmi Chikkamma. 'She has to get very close without being noticed, and then rush. Once the deer have seen her, a chase would only waste her energy. A good hunter knows when to stop. She will try again somewhere else, perhaps tonight.'
'So the deer won,' said Arun.

'Today,' said Lakshmi Chikkamma. 'Tomorrow the tiger may win. She has to eat too. If tigers never caught a deer, there would be no tigers. If tigers caught every deer, there would soon be no deer, and then no tigers either.'
On the way back they passed the nightjar again, still as a leaf. This time Arun saw her first. 'I looked for the eye,' he said proudly. 'Meenakshi taught me.'

That night, at the forest quarters, a house gecko sat very still on the wall beside the tube light. A moth fluttered close. The gecko waited, and waited, and then darted. Meenakshi laughed. 'Look, Arun,' she said. 'A tiny tiger. She hunts by waiting too.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: the nightjar and the tiger were both hidden by camouflage, because their colours and patterns matched the dry leaves and grass where they lay. Meenakshi found them by looking for what did not match: a shiny eye, a stripe curving the wrong way, an ear that moved. The chital graze for most of the day because grass gives little energy, so they eat in a herd, where many eyes keep watch, and they feed near langurs, who see far from the treetops. Once the alarm calls showed the tiger that she had been seen, her ambush could no longer work, so she gave up rather than waste energy on a chase. Most hunts fail. Tigers need deer to eat, but if tigers caught every deer, there would soon be no deer, and then no tigers either.
ask: How did the nightjar stay safe without a nest?
What trick did Meenakshi use to find the nightjar and the tiger?
Why did the chital graze under the langurs' tree?
Why did the tiger walk away without chasing the deer?
Arun knew a lot from films, but Meenakshi spotted the animals first. What did she do that he did not?

printables.title: 4 pile labels
items: HUNTS (chases, waits in ambush or sets a trap)
STAYS SAFE (hides, keeps still, armour, a group)

rules: Cut out the 20 animal cards and the 4 pile labels. Lay the 4 labels in a row on the floor.
Shuffle the animal cards and put them face down in a pile.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud. Put it on the pile you think is right, and say why.
Turn the card over to check. If you were right, keep the card as a point. If not, put the card at the bottom of the face-down pile, so that it comes up again later.
Playing alone? Read each card, choose a pile, then turn it over to check.
The game ends when every card has been won. The player with the most cards wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and the 4 labels. 2. Lay the labels in a row. 3. Shuffle the animal cards face down.
flow.say: Every animal has to eat, and stay safe. Each card shows one animal doing one of these. Which pile does the card go on?
flow.kid: Lay out the 4 labels. Mix up the cards. Each card shows an animal eating or staying safe. Which pile?
flow.context: This is the first step of Hunt, Graze or Hide? Here you set out the four piles and the animal cards.

flow.do: Read the practice card 'A house gecko waits beside the tube light for moths' together.
flow.say: Practice card. A house gecko waits beside the tube light for moths. Which pile?
flow.kid: Practice card. A gecko waits by the tube light for moths. Which pile?

check.q: A house gecko waits beside the tube light for moths. Which pile?
check.why: The gecko is a predator who waits for moths to come close, then darts. That is hunting by ambush. Picking 'stays safe' is a fair guess, because the gecko keeps still. But here she keeps still to catch food.

flow.do: Take turns reading and placing the cards until every card is won.
flow.say: Your turn. Read the card, choose a pile, and tell us why.
flow.kid: Take a card. Read it out. Choose a pile. Say why. Turn it over to check.
flow.parent: Some cards fit two piles. The nightjar keeps still and is camouflaged. The kingfisher waits, then dives. Let your child argue for their choice. A good reason counts.

flow.do: Ask the question below once the game is over.
flow.say: Which pile had the most cards? Was there a card you could have put in two piles?
flow.kid: Which pile was biggest? Which card could go in two piles? Why?

ask.q: Which animal could go in two piles?
good: The frog, who keeps still to stay safe and is also a hunter.
The crow, who scavenges and also hunts insects.

games.title: Freeze, Tiger!
games.context: This is a running and freezing game. Deer collect grass while a tiger tries to catch them moving. It shows why prey keep still, and why eating in the open is risky.
rules: You need 30 paper strips scattered on the floor as grass (cut them from old newspaper), and a cushion at one end of the room as the waterhole.
One player is the tiger. The tiger stands at the waterhole, facing the wall.
Everyone else is a deer, starting at the other end of the room.
While the tiger faces the wall, deer move forward and pick up grass, one strip at a time.
The tiger can turn round at any moment. When she turns, every deer must freeze.
If the tiger sees a deer moving, that deer is caught and goes back to the start without their grass.
The round ends when a deer touches the waterhole. Count each deer's grass. Swap who is the tiger.

After three rounds, add up each deer's grass. The deer with the most grass wins. Playing with two, swap roles after each round so that each of you is the tiger at least once, and compare totals at the end.
Playing with just one grown-up? The grown-up is the tiger, and the child plays three rounds as the deer. The aim is to beat your own total from the round before.

flow.do: 1. Scatter 30 paper strips on the floor as grass. 2. Put a cushion at the far end as the waterhole. 3. Choose a tiger.
flow.say: Deer must eat, but every step in the open is a risk. Grab grass while the tiger isn't looking. Freeze when she turns!
flow.kid: You are a deer. Pick up grass and move to the waterhole. When the tiger turns, freeze!
flow.context: This is the first step of Freeze, Tiger! You set out paper grass and a waterhole, and choose a tiger.

flow.do: Play three rounds. After each round, write how many strips of grass each deer collected, and whether they were caught.
flow.say: Tiger, face the wall. Deer, go! Remember to freeze.
flow.kid: Go! Pick up grass. Freeze when the tiger turns. Don't wobble!
flow.parent: As the tiger, turn round at uneven times. Sometimes quickly, sometimes after a long wait. That is what makes freezing hard.

flow.do: Ask the questions below after the last round.
flow.say: Did the deer who collected the most grass get caught more often? Why?
flow.kid: Did grabbing lots of grass make you easier to catch? Why?

check.q: In the game, why were deer who kept moving caught more often?
options: The tiger noticed movement, even when the deer were far away
Moving deer were a different colour
The tiger could only see deer who had grass
check.why: Eyes notice movement quickly. A deer who freezes is much harder to spot. Real prey face the same choice: every moment spent eating in the open is a moment they might be seen. Picking 'a different colour' is not right, because every player looked the same in every round.

setup.caption: 1. Scatter paper grass. The tiger faces the wall.

setup.caption: 2. Deer collect grass and freeze when the tiger turns.

experiments.title: Paper Caterpillars: which ones does a hungry hunter miss?
experiments.question: Do prey that match the background survive a hunter better than prey that stand out? And what happens when the background changes?
experiments.predict: Guess first. On a newspaper, will you catch more newspaper strips or more plain strips in 20 seconds? On a plain sheet, which kind will you catch more of? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use 20 strips of each kind, all the same size. Hunt for the same time, 20 seconds, with one hand, one strip at a time. Someone else scatters the strips while the hunter's eyes are closed. Do 3 rounds on each background, because one round can be a fluke. Only the background changes.

materials.item: two sheets of old newspaper with lots of small print: one to cut and one to spread on the floor
two sheets of plain paper, all one colour, such as white paper or an old notebook page
a plain background the same colour as the plain paper, such as a white bedsheet, a plain dupatta or a sheet of chart paper
scissors
a small bowl or cup to drop the strips into
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand

schedule.what: Cut 40 paper caterpillars. Hunt them for 20 seconds on a newspaper, 3 times, then on a plain sheet, 3 times. Compare the counts.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart with two bars for each background: newspaper strips caught and plain strips caught.

flow.do: 1. Fold one newspaper sheet into four layers. 2. Cut strips about 3 cm long and 1 cm wide, through all four layers. 3. Stop when you have 20 newspaper strips. 4. Do the same with the plain paper, to make 20 plain strips. 5. Keep all 40 strips about the same size.
flow.say: These strips are caterpillars, and you are a hungry bird. Some caterpillars match the newspaper and some don't.
flow.kid: Fold the newspaper. Cut 20 small strips. Cut 20 strips of plain paper too. Make them all the same size. These are your caterpillars.
flow.parent: Cutting through four layers saves time. The strips do not need to be perfect. Choose plain paper the same colour as your plain background, for example white strips and a white bedsheet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Paper Caterpillars experiment. Here you make 40 paper prey: 20 that match a newspaper and 20 that do not.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason before any hunting. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: On the newspaper, which caterpillars will you catch more of? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. On the newspaper, which strips will you catch more of? Why?

ask.q: Which caterpillars will you catch more of on the newspaper, and why?
good: The plain ones, because they stand out.
Fewer newspaper ones, because they look like the background.

flow.do: 1. Spread the second newspaper flat on the floor. 2. The hunter closes their eyes. 3. Scatter all 40 strips over the newspaper, well mixed. 4. Say 'Go!' and start a 20-second timer. 5. The hunter picks up strips one at a time with one hand. 6. Each strip goes into the bowl before the next. 7. Say 'Stop!' at 20 seconds.
flow.say: Close your eyes while I scatter the caterpillars. Ready? Pick them up one at a time, as fast as you can. Go!
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Wait for 'Go!' Pick up one strip at a time. Drop each one in the bowl. Be quick! Stop at 20 seconds.
flow.parent: One hand and one strip at a time is like a bird pecking one insect at a time. It keeps every round fair. Stand up while hunting, so you look down from the same height each time.

flow.do: 1. Count the newspaper strips and the plain strips in the bowl. 2. Write both numbers in the table. 3. Put all 40 strips back on the newspaper. 4. Do 2 more rounds, so there are 3 rounds in all.
flow.say: Let's count what you caught. Then we'll hunt twice more, because one round could be a fluke.
flow.kid: Count each kind in your bowl. Write the numbers. Put them all back. Hunt 2 more times.

check.q: On the newspaper, which caterpillars were left behind most?
options: The newspaper strips, because they matched the background
The plain strips, because they were harder to pick up
check.why: The newspaper strips had the same grey print as the background, so your eyes skipped over them. That is camouflage. If you picked 'the plain strips', count again: most hunters catch far more plain strips. If the numbers were nearly the same, the plain paper may be a colour that blends in. Try whiter paper.

flow.do: 1. Take away the newspaper and spread the plain sheet on the floor. 2. Ask for a new guess and a reason. 3. Scatter all 40 strips on it while the hunter's eyes are closed. 4. Hunt for 20 seconds, 3 rounds, as before. 5. Write the numbers each time.
flow.say: Now the caterpillars are on a plain sheet, not a newspaper. Which kind will you catch more of now? Why?
flow.kid: Now hunt on the plain sheet. Guess first. Which kind will you catch more now? Why? Hunt 3 times. Write the numbers.

ask.q: What changed between the two hunts?
good: The strips were the same, but the place under them was different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A strong answer sounds like this. What I think: prey that match the background are harder for a hunter to find. What I saw: on the newspaper I caught about 15 plain strips and only 3 newspaper strips. On the plain sheet it was the other way round. Why: the newspaper strips matched the newspaper, so my eyes missed them. On the plain sheet they did not match, so they stood out.

experiments.context: In this experiment you are a hungry bird hunting paper caterpillars. You find out which ones a hunter misses, and whether it changes when the background changes.

experiments.title: Still or Moving: which caterpillar do eyes find first?
experiments.question: Does a hunter spot hidden prey sooner when the prey moves than when the prey keeps still?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will you spot a newspaper caterpillar on a newspaper faster if the strip keeps still, or if the strip wriggles a little? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same newspaper strip on the same newspaper every time, so it is always equally well hidden. Only one thing changes: whether the strip moves. The hunter stands in the same place each time. Do 3 tries of each, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a newspaper spread on the floor
one newspaper strip, about 3 cm by 1 cm, from the Paper Caterpillars experiment
a piece of light-coloured thread, about 60 cm long, and a little sticky tape
a pencil, to poke small holes
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand

schedule.what: Time how long it takes to spot a still newspaper strip on a newspaper, then a wriggling one. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Add up the three still times and the three wriggling times, and compare them.

flow.do: 1. Spread a newspaper on the floor. 2. Poke 3 small holes in it with a pencil, far apart. 3. Tape one end of a 60 cm thread to the end of a newspaper strip.
flow.say: We are making a caterpillar that can wriggle. The thread will run under the paper, so the hunter won't see you pull it.
flow.kid: Help tape a thread to the end of one newspaper strip. The thread will go down through a hole and under the paper. Then the strip can wriggle.
flow.parent: Use a light-coloured thread. Sit at the side of the newspaper and keep your hand still under the edge, so the hunter cannot see where you pull from.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Still or Moving experiment. You make a hidden paper caterpillar that can move, to test whether moving gives prey away.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Will you spot a hidden caterpillar faster if the strip keeps still, or if the strip wriggles a little? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Still or wriggling: which will you spot faster? Why?

flow.do: 1. The hunter stands one big step from the newspaper and turns round. 2. Lay the strip on the newspaper about 2 cm from one hole, with the taped end nearer the hole. 3. Push the thread down through that hole and under the newspaper to where you sit. 4. Say 'Look!' and start the timer. 5. Stop the timer when the hunter points at the strip. 6. Do this 3 times, using a different hole each time. Keep the strip still every time.
flow.say: Turn round. Now look! Point the moment you spot the strip.
flow.kid: Turn round. When you hear 'Look!', search for the strip. Point the moment you spot the strip.
flow.parent: If your child takes longer than 30 seconds, write 'more than 30' and move on.

flow.do: 1. Do 3 more tries, using the holes in a new order and threading the strip each time. 2. This time, give the thread a small tug about once every two seconds, so the strip jerks a little. 3. Time how long the hunter takes to point.
flow.say: Turn round again. Same game, but this time the caterpillar might be wriggling. Look!
flow.kid: Turn round. Look again. Point the moment you spot the strip.

check.q: Which caterpillar did you usually spot faster?
check.why: Eyes are very quick to notice movement, even when the colour matches. That is why many prey animals freeze when danger is near. If you spotted the still strip faster, check that the strip had not landed on a white gap in the newspaper.

flow.do: Ask your child for three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this. What I think: moving gives hidden prey away. What I saw: the still strip took me 12, 9 and 15 seconds to find, but the wriggling one took only 2, 1 and 3 seconds. Why: my eyes noticed the movement straight away, even though the colour matched.

experiments.context: In this experiment you find out whether moving gives a hidden animal away, by timing how fast you spot a still or a wriggling paper caterpillar.

activities.title: Graze or Hunt? A one-minute food race

materials.item: about 2 tablespoons of raw rice, spread on a steel plate
5 rajma beans, or 5 groundnuts
2 small cups or bowls
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand

schedule.what: Pick rice grains from a plate for 30 seconds, like a grazer. Then hunt for 5 hidden beans for 30 seconds, like a hunter. Compare.

activities.record: Write how many rice grains you picked and how many beans you found.
activities.context: This is a quick race to start the unit. You feed like a grazer, then like a hunter, and find out why the two eat so differently.

flow.do: 1. Spread the rice on the plate. 2. Say 'Go!' and start a 30-second timer. 3. Your child picks up grains one at a time and drops them in a cup. 4. Say 'Stop!' and count the grains together.
flow.say: You are a cow, and this rice is grass. Grass is everywhere, so you just keep picking. Go!
flow.kid: You are a cow. The rice is grass. Pick up one grain at a time. Drop it in the cup. Go!
flow.context: This is the first part of Graze or Hunt. Here you feed like a grazer, from food that is all around you.

flow.do: 1. Send your child out of the room. 2. Hide 5 beans in different places in the room, a little out of sight. 3. Call your child back and start a 30-second timer. 4. Count the beans found.
flow.say: Now you are a tiger. Your food is hidden and rare. You have 30 seconds to find it. Go!
flow.kid: Now you are a tiger. Five beans are hiding in this room. Find as many as you can. Go!
flow.parent: Hide the beans well enough that finding them takes a little searching, for example under the edge of a mat or behind a cushion. Most children find 2 or 3 in 30 seconds.

flow.do: 1. Put the rice grains in one palm and the beans in the other. 2. Ask which hand holds more food. 3. Tell your child that one rajma bean weighs about as much as 20 rice grains.
flow.say: You picked lots of rice, but each grain is tiny. You found only a few beans, but each one is big. Which hand has more food?
flow.kid: Hold the rice in one hand and the beans in the other. Which hand has more food? One bean weighs about the same as 20 rice grains.

ask.q: Why does a cow eat for most of the day, but a tiger does not?
good: Grass is everywhere but each bite gives little food, so the cow must keep eating.
Meat is hard to find, but each catch is a big meal.

check.q: Grass is easy to find. So why do cows spend most of the day eating?
options: Each mouthful gives little energy, so they need a lot
check.why: Grass is all around, but each bite gives little energy and is slow to digest. So a grazer must eat a great deal. Picking 'greedy' blames the cow, but every grazer needs that much food. Picking 'hard to find' mixes up grazers with hunters, whose food is hard to find.

activities.title: Shadow Belly: why so many animals have a pale belly

materials.item: 2 empty toilet roll tubes, or 2 sheets of white paper rolled into tubes and taped
a pencil or a grey or brown crayon
a torch, or the ceiling light of a room
a sheet of plain grey or brown paper, or a plain table top

schedule.what: Shade the top half of one tube. Light both tubes from above and compare how round and how easy to see they look.

activities.record: Draw both tubes as they looked from the side, with the light above.
activities.context: In this activity you find out why many fish, deer and birds are darker on top and paler underneath. This is called countershading.

flow.do: 1. Leave one tube plain white. 2. Shade the top half of the other tube evenly with pencil or crayon. 3. Leave its bottom half white.
flow.say: Many fish are dark on top and pale underneath. Let's make a tube like that, and one that is plain.
flow.kid: Keep one tube white. Colour the top half of the other tube grey. Leave the bottom white.
flow.context: This is the first step of Shadow Belly. You make two paper animals: one plain, one darker on top.

flow.do: 1. Lay both tubes on their sides on the plain paper. 2. Make the light shine from straight above, with the torch or the ceiling light. 3. Crouch down so your eyes are level with the tubes.
flow.say: Light comes from the sky, from above. Look from the side, like a hunter on the ground. Which tube looks round, and which looks flat?
flow.kid: Lay the tubes down. Shine the light from above. Crouch down low. Which tube looks round? Which looks flat?

ask.q: Where is the plain tube darkest?
good: At the bottom, where the light does not reach.

flow.do: Turn the shaded tube upside down, so the dark half is underneath. Look again from the side.
flow.say: Now the dark side is at the bottom. Does it look flatter or rounder than before?
flow.kid: Turn the grey tube upside down. Now does it look flat or round?

check.q: Why does a dark back and a pale belly help a fish hide?
options: The pale belly evens out the shadow underneath, so the body looks flat
A pale belly makes the fish swim faster
check.why: Light from above makes the top of a body bright and the bottom dark. A darker back and a paler belly even this out, so the body looks flat and blends in. Hunters often find prey by the shading that shows a round shape. Picking 'dark colours are invisible' is a natural guess, but dark things can be easy to see on a pale background.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they saw and why, in two or three sentences.
flow.say: Tell me what you saw. Why do you think so many fish and deer have pale bellies?
flow.kid: Say what you saw. Why do fish and deer have pale bellies?
flow.parent: The difference is real but small. It is clearest with one light directly above and the room otherwise dim. A good answer: the white tube had a dark shadow underneath, so it looked round. The shaded tube looked flatter, because its dark top and pale bottom evened out the light.

activities.title: Hide a Paper Animal in Your Home

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper
crayons, colour pencils or sketch pens
scissors
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand

schedule.what: Choose a spot at home, design a paper animal coloured to match that spot, and see how long the family takes to find them. Then move the animal to the wrong spot.

activities.record: Write how long the family took to find your animal in the right spot and in the wrong spot.
activities.context: In this activity you design your own camouflaged animal for one spot in your home, and test how well they hide.

flow.do: 1. Walk around the home with your child. 2. Help them choose one spot with a pattern or colour. 3. A bedsheet, a curtain, a doormat, floor tiles or a bookshelf all work.
flow.say: Choose a home for your animal. It needs a colour or pattern you can copy.
flow.kid: Walk around your home. Choose a place with a pattern or colour. Your animal will hide there.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hide a Paper Animal. You choose a place in your home for a camouflaged animal to live.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws an animal about as big as a matchbox. 2. They colour the animal to match the chosen spot. 3. They cut the animal out.
flow.say: Look closely at the colours and lines in that spot. Copy them onto your animal.
flow.kid: Draw an animal as big as a matchbox. Colour them to match your spot. Copy the lines and spots too. Cut them out.

flow.do: 1. Everyone else leaves the room. 2. Your child places the animal on the chosen spot. 3. Each person gets up to one minute to find the animal, timed.
flow.say: Let's see how well your animal hides. I'll time each person.
flow.kid: Hide your animal on your spot. Time each person. How long do they take to find your animal?

flow.do: 1. Now place the animal on a spot that does not match. 2. Time the search again.
flow.say: Now let's put your animal in the wrong home. How long does the search take now?
flow.kid: Now put your animal somewhere that does not match. Time the search again. What changed?

ask.q: Why was your animal found faster in the wrong spot?
good: The colours did not match the background any more.
Camouflage only works in the right place.

activities.title: The Antlion's Trap: a pit of rava

materials.item: a deep steel bowl or a small steel plate with a rim
about 2 cups of dry rava (sooji), or fine dry sand
a spoon
a few grains of raw rice, to be the ants

schedule.what: Make a cone-shaped pit in dry rava, like an antlion's trap, and watch rice grain 'ants' slide down into it.

activities.record: Draw the pit from the side and show where the antlion waits.
activities.context: In this activity you build a trap like the pit of an antlion, a young insect who hunts by digging a pit in dry sand.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bowl with dry rava, about 4 cm deep. 2. With the spoon, scoop rava out of the middle and flick it over the side. 3. Keep scooping until you have a cone-shaped pit with steep, loose sides.
flow.say: An antlion is the young of a winged insect. They dig a pit in dry sand by flicking it out, just like this.
flow.kid: Fill the bowl with rava. Scoop rava out of the middle. Flick it away. Make a pit like a cone.
flow.parent: Loose rava settles into sides that are as steep as they can be, so the smallest push makes them slide. Rava gives a neat pit. Sand works too, but it must be completely dry.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Antlion's Trap. You dig a cone-shaped pit like an antlion's.

flow.do: 1. Put a rice grain 'ant' near the top edge of the pit. 2. Nudge it gently towards the middle with a fingertip. 3. Watch the rava slide and carry the grain down.
flow.say: This rice grain is an ant, walking along. Let's see what happens at the edge of the pit.
flow.kid: Put a rice grain at the edge. Push it gently to the middle. Where does the grain end up?

ask.q: Why can't the ant climb back out?
good: The loose sides slide down under the ant's feet.
Every step makes more rava fall into the pit.

flow.do: Tell your child what a real antlion does, then ask the question below.
flow.say: A real antlion waits buried at the bottom, with only her jaws showing. If an ant starts to climb out, she flicks sand at the ant. Is a trap a good way to hunt?
flow.kid: A real antlion waits at the bottom. If the ant climbs, she flicks sand. Is a trap a good way to hunt? Why?
flow.parent: Antlion pits are common in India in dry dust under shelter, for example under the eaves of old buildings or temple walls. If you have a park or a courtyard nearby, look for little cone-shaped pits about as wide as a coin. Rava can be sieved and used for cooking afterwards.

activities.title: How Often Do They Look Up? Watch a feeding flock

materials.item: a window or balcony where pigeons, mynas, sparrows or crows come to feed
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand
a notebook and pencil

schedule.what: If you can see birds feeding, count how often one bird looks up in a minute. Do it for a bird in a big group and a bird alone or in a small group.

activities.record: Write how many times the bird looked up in one minute, and how many birds were in the group.
activities.context: In this activity you watch birds feeding, if you can see some, and count how often they stop to look for danger.

flow.do: 1. Find a spot where birds feed, such as pigeons on a road or a terrace, or birds at a feeder. 2. Watch quietly from a window, so the birds are not disturbed.
flow.say: Let's watch how birds eat. Every so often they stop eating and lift their head to look around.
flow.kid: Look out of the window. Find birds who are eating. Watch them quietly.
flow.parent: This works only if birds come where you can see them. Pigeons are easiest in most Indian cities. If no birds come, skip this activity and play Freeze, Tiger! instead.
flow.context: This is the first step of the flock watch. You find birds who are feeding, to watch how often they look up.

flow.do: 1. Pick one bird in a big group. 2. Start a one-minute timer. 3. Your child counts how many times that bird lifts their head to look around.
flow.say: Choose one bird in the big group. Count each time they lift their head. Go!
flow.kid: Pick one bird in a big group. Count each time they look up. Stop after one minute.

flow.do: 1. Now pick a bird who is feeding alone or with only one or two others. 2. Count how many times they lift their head in one minute. 3. Compare the two numbers.
flow.say: Now a bird with fewer friends. Who looks up more?
flow.kid: Now pick a bird who is alone, or nearly alone. Count again. Who looked up more?

ask.q: Why might a bird in a big group look up less?
good: Many eyes keep watch, so each bird can eat more.

projects.title: Home Hunters Diary

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a torch
a crumb of biscuit or a few grains of cooked rice

schedule.what: After dark, watch the wall near a lit tube light or bulb for 10 minutes. Note insects and any house gecko, and where the gecko waits.
Look for spider webs in corners, window grilles and the balcony. Draw one web and anything caught in it.
Put a biscuit crumb on a window ledge or balcony. Check after 10 minutes and again later. Who came to forage?

projects.record: Each day, write the date, the time, who you saw, and what they were doing to get food.
projects.context: In this 3-day project you look for the hunters and foragers who share your home: geckos, spiders, ants and birds.

flow.do: 1. After dark, switch on a tube light or bulb near a wall or window. 2. Sit quietly a little way off for 10 minutes. 3. Count the insects near the light. 4. Look for a house gecko and note where they wait.
flow.say: Hunters go where the food is. Insects fly to the light at night. Who comes to hunt them?
flow.kid: Sit near the light. Stay quiet. Count the insects. Is there a gecko? Where does the gecko wait?
flow.parent: House geckos are common in most Indian homes and stairwells, but not every home has one. If you see none inside, look on an outside wall near a lit window or the stairwell light.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Home Hunters Diary. Tonight you watch a light, where insects gather and hunters wait.

flow.do: 1. In daylight, check corners, window grilles, the balcony and behind furniture for spider webs. 2. Shine the torch along a web to see the threads. 3. Draw one web and anything caught in it.
flow.say: A spider builds a trap and waits. Let's find a web and see what she caught.
flow.kid: Look in corners and window grilles. Find a spider web. Draw it. Is anything caught?
flow.parent: Look, but don't touch. Most house spiders are harmless, but it is kind to leave their webs in place.

flow.do: 1. Put a crumb of biscuit on a window ledge or balcony. 2. Check after 10 minutes. 3. Check again in the evening. 4. Write who came: ants, a crow, a sparrow, a myna, or nobody yet.
flow.say: Let's put out a little food and see who forages for it.
flow.kid: Put a crumb on the window ledge. Check after 10 minutes. Who came to eat?

ask.q: Who hunted, who scavenged, and who waited in your home this week?
good: The gecko waited by the light, which is an ambush.
Ants or crows scavenged the crumb.

challenges.title: A Feeder for Small Beaks
challenges.problem: When grain is put out for small birds such as sparrows, bigger birds such as crows and pigeons often eat most of it. Design a feeder from a plastic bottle that a small beak can reach into, but a big beak cannot.
constraints: A pencil is the small beak. A thick marker pen is the big beak.
The small beak must reach the grain. The big beak must not.
The feeder must not hurt any bird: no sharp edges and no wire loops.
materials: an empty plastic bottle with its cap
a pencil and a thick marker pen
some grain, such as bajra or broken rice
general: Cut feeding holes just big enough for the pencil, but too small for the marker.
Put a short perch under each hole, so only light birds can hold on.
Hang the feeder on a string, so it swings. Heavy birds find it harder to land on.
creative: Make a cage of ice-cream sticks or rolled paper around the feeder, with gaps a sparrow can slip through but a crow cannot.
Put the holes low on the bottle and fill it with only a little grain, so a beak has to reach deep inside to get any.
Make a feeder that hangs under a small roof, so big birds cannot land on top.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own small-beak feeder. Draw it, build it, and test it with the pencil and the marker. If you can, hang it at a window and watch who comes.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about foraging. Birds compete for food, and you design a feeder that lets small birds eat.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the pencil and the marker. 2. Explain the problem.
flow.say: Big birds often eat all the grain before sparrows get any. Can you make a feeder only a small beak can use?
flow.kid: The pencil is a sparrow's beak. The marker is a crow's beak. Make a feeder only the pencil can reach into.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Small Beaks challenge. Here you see the problem and the two test beaks.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a design. 2. Together, mark the holes. 3. A grown-up cuts the holes with scissors. 4. Smooth any sharp edges with tape.
flow.say: Draw your idea first. Then we'll make the holes together. I'll do the cutting.
flow.kid: Draw your feeder. Mark where the holes go. A grown-up cuts them. Cover sharp edges with tape.
flow.parent: Cutting plastic bottles leaves sharp edges. Make a small cut with the scissor tip, then widen the hole slowly. Cover every edge with tape, for the birds' safety and yours.

flow.do: 1. Put a little grain in the bottle. 2. Test each hole with the pencil and the marker. 3. Change any hole that is too big or too small.
flow.say: Test time. Can the pencil reach the grain? Can the marker?
flow.kid: Put in some grain. Push the pencil into each hole. Now the marker. Which one reaches the grain?

check.q: The marker can still reach the grain through one hole. What should you change?
options: Make that hole smaller, or cover part of it with tape
check.why: A smaller hole lets the pencil in but keeps the marker out. Bigger holes would let big beaks in. Adding grain does not change who can reach it.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain their design in two or three sentences.
flow.say: Tell me how your feeder works, and why a crow would struggle with your feeder.
flow.kid: Say how your feeder works. Why can't a big beak use it?
