quiz.p: Which word means searching for food and getting it?
quiz.why: To forage is to search for food and get it. Hibernating is a long winter rest, migrating is travelling far, and camouflage is hiding by matching the place.

quiz.p: A spider spins a sticky web and waits. How is she hunting?
quiz.why: The web is a trap that catches insects for her. She does not chase them.

quiz.p: A mugger crocodile lies still in a river, with only her eyes above the water. How is she hunting?
quiz.why: She waits, still and hidden, until an animal comes to drink. That is an ambush.

quiz.p: Why does an elephant feed for most of the day and part of the night?
opts: Leaves and grass give little energy in each mouthful
There is very little food in a forest
Elephants waste most of their food
quiz.why: Plants give little energy in each mouthful, and a big body needs a lot. So elephants spend most of their time eating.

quiz.p: Newspaper strips and plain white strips are scattered on a sheet of newspaper. A hunter picks them up as fast as she can. Which strips will she most likely miss?
quiz.why: The newspaper strips match the background, so the hunter's eyes pass over them. That is camouflage. The plain strips stand out, so they are found first.

quiz.p: Newspaper strips were hard to find on a newspaper. Then the same strips were moved onto a plain white sheet. What happened?
opts: They were even harder to find
quiz.why: On the white sheet the grey print no longer matched, so the strips stood out. Camouflage depends on the place.

quiz.p: Why do chital listen for langur alarm calls?
opts: Langurs sit high in trees and can see a tiger or leopard from far away
Langurs tell the chital where grass is
quiz.why: From the treetops, langurs see far. Their alarm calls warn the chital below, who look up and get ready to run.

quiz.p: A tortoise pulls her head and legs into her shell. How is she staying safe?
quiz.why: The hard shell is armour. Many hunters cannot bite through it.

quiz.p: Why is keeping still a good way to stay hidden?
opts: Moving makes an animal change colour
quiz.why: Eyes notice movement quickly. A still animal who matches the background is much harder to find, as the Still or Moving test showed.

quiz.p: Over a very long time, what happens when prey get better at hiding?
opts: The hunters who survive are the ones better at finding them
The prey stop needing to hide
quiz.why: Hunters who cannot find enough food have fewer young. So, over many generations, hunters and prey change together.

quiz.p: A crow eats rice, fruit, insects and a dead rat. What kind of eater is the crow?
quiz.why: Crows eat plants and animals, and also eat animals that are already dead. That makes them omnivores and scavengers.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: Exactly what a deer sees and feels when a tiger is near
quiz.why: Nobody can look out through a deer's eyes. Scientists study deer eyes and behaviour, but what the deer feels is still debated.

items.p: A buffalo grazes beside a canal for most of the day. Why does she eat for so long?
opts: Grass gives little energy in each mouthful, so she needs a lot
She has nothing else to do
items.why: Grass is easy to find, but each mouthful gives little energy and is slow to digest. So a grazer must eat a great deal. A strong answer does not blame the buffalo: every grazer needs that much.

items.p: A pond heron stands still at the edge of a pond for a long time. Then the heron stabs the water. How is the heron hunting?
opts: By ambush: waiting still, then striking
items.why: The heron waits, still and hidden, until a fish comes close, then strikes. That is an ambush. A chaser would run or fly after the fish, and a trapper would build something.

items.p: An animal who hunts and eats other animals is called a ____.
items.why: A predator hunts other animals. The animals a predator hunts are called prey.

items.p: Colour or pattern that makes a body hard to see against the place where they are is called ____.
items.why: Camouflage is a match between a body and the place. In the Paper Caterpillars test, the newspaper strips were camouflaged on the newspaper.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: eats animals that are already dead
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words describe what an animal eats. A strong answer could give an example of each: a cow, a tiger, a crow, a vulture and a deer.

items.p: Sort these animals: does each one hunt other animals, or eat plants?
items.a: see items
items.why: Tigers, spiders, kingfishers and geckos are predators. Cows, goats, elephants and chital are herbivores who graze or browse.

items.p: A tiger catches nearly every animal she chases.
items.why: False. Most of a tiger's hunts fail, because deer often see, hear or smell her first. A strong answer gives a reason, such as the chital's alarm calls.

items.p: Keeping still helps a camouflaged animal stay hidden.
items.why: True. Many hunters notice movement first. In the Still or Moving test, the wriggling strip was spotted much faster than the still one.

items.p: In your Paper Caterpillars test on the newspaper, which strips did you catch the most of? Explain why, using the word 'camouflage'.
items.a: I caught the most plain strips. The newspaper strips had camouflage, because they matched the newspaper, so my eyes missed them.
items.why: A strong answer gives the numbers from the test and says the newspaper strips matched the background.

items.p: Why do chital deer graze in a herd and not alone? Give two reasons.
items.a: In a herd there are many eyes and ears, so someone notices a tiger sooner. Each deer can spend more time eating and less time looking up.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different reasons, such as more eyes keeping watch and more time to eat, or an alarm call warning everyone.

items.p: Draw a moth on a tree trunk, coloured so that a bird would find her hard to see. Then draw the same moth on a white wall.
items.a: Two drawings: a moth with bark-like colours and lines on a tree trunk, and the same moth standing out on a white wall.
items.why: A strong drawing copies the bark's colours and cracks onto the moth, and shows that on the white wall the same moth is easy to see.
items.art: An empty tree trunk outline on the left and an empty white wall on the right.

items.p: Put the steps of the Paper Caterpillars test in order.
items: Hunt for 20 seconds, one strip at a time
Scatter the strips while the hunter's eyes are closed
Cut 20 newspaper strips and 20 plain strips
Count how many of each kind were caught
a: Cut 20 newspaper strips and 20 plain strips
Scatter the strips while the hunter's eyes are closed
Hunt for 20 seconds, one strip at a time
Count how many of each kind were caught
items.why: First make the prey, then hide them fairly, then hunt, then count.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out?
opts: A tortoise pulling into her shell
A pangolin rolling into a ball
items.why: The tortoise, the pangolin and the porcupine are all staying safe. The dhole is hunting.

items.p: Two friends in Hyderabad watch a film of a tiger chasing a deer.

views.says: I want the deer to escape. It is not fair that the tiger hunts.
I want the tiger to win. She has cubs to feed, and she might be very hungry.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you learned about how often a tiger's hunts fail. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence, such as most tiger hunts failing, or the cubs needing food. It also sees the other side: the deer wants to live too, or the tiger has to eat.
items.why: Both friends are right about something. A tiger has to eat to live, and a deer escapes most hunts. A strong answer uses a fact from the unit, not just a feeling.

items.p: Which of these animals is a scavenger?
opts: A vulture eating a cow who has died
A spider waiting in her web
items.why: A scavenger eats animals that are already dead. The goat is a browser, the spider is a trapper, and the flamingo filters food from water.

items.p: A goat browses and a buffalo grazes. What is the difference?
items.a: A goat browses: she eats leaves and twigs from bushes and trees. A buffalo grazes: she eats grass and low plants on the ground.
items.why: A strong answer says where each animal finds their food: up on bushes, or low on the ground.

items.p: In the Still or Moving test, the wriggling strip was spotted much sooner. What does this tell you about how prey stay alive?
opts: Keeping still can save a prey animal's life
Colour does not matter at all
items.why: Eyes notice movement quickly, so prey who freeze are harder to find. Moving fast can help once you have been seen, but not before.

items.p: A green leaf insect is put on a white wall. What happens?
opts: She becomes easy to see, because her green no longer matches
items.why: Camouflage works only against the right background. Leaf insects cannot change their colour, so on a white wall the match is gone.

items.p: Many fish, such as the mackerel, are dark blue on top and silvery white underneath. Explain how this helps them hide. Use the word 'countershading'.
items.a: This is countershading. Light from above makes the top of the fish bright and the belly dark with shadow. The dark back and pale belly even this out, so the fish looks flat and blends in.
items.why: A strong answer mentions the light coming from above and the shadow underneath. The Shadow Belly tubes show it.

items.p: A tiger creeps close to a herd of chital. The chital see her and give alarm calls. Why might the tiger give up instead of chasing?
items.a: Her hunt works by surprise. Once the deer have seen her, they will run as soon as she rushes, so a chase would waste her energy. She will try again later.
items.why: A strong answer says that ambush needs surprise, and that chasing costs a lot of energy.

items.p: Chital deer often graze under trees where langur monkeys are feeding. Two people explain why.

views.says: The langurs help the deer. They drop leaves for them, and their alarm calls warn the deer about tigers.
The langurs are not trying to help anyone. They drop leaves by accident, and they call to warn their own troop. The deer just listen in.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Can both be right? Then think about the langurs: do they gain anything from having deer nearby?
items.a: A strong answer sees that both can be partly right: the deer gain food and warnings, whether or not the langurs mean to help. It may add that langurs gain too, because chital have a good sense of smell and give alarm calls from the ground.
items.why: Scientists think both animals gain from feeding together. Whether the langurs 'mean' to help is a harder question. A strong answer separates what happens from what anyone intends.

items.p: Animals in a big flock each spend more time looking up for danger than an animal feeding alone.
items.why: False. In bigger groups each animal looks up less often, because many others are watching too. So each one can eat more.

items.p: A peacock's long, bright tail helps him hide from tigers.
items.why: False. Not every colour is for hiding. A peacock's tail is for showing off to peahens. The plain brown peahen, who sits on the eggs, is much better hidden.

items.p: Put the steps of a tiger's hunt by ambush in order.
items: Freezes whenever a deer looks up
Creeps closer, keeping low in the grass
a: Creeps closer, keeping low in the grass
Freezes whenever a deer looks up
items.why: An ambush needs the tiger to get very close without being seen. She creeps and freezes in turn, and rushes only at the end.

items.p: Sort these: does each animal stay safe by camouflage, or in another way?
items: an oakleaf butterfly with closed wings
a chital listening for alarm calls
a pangolin rolled into a ball
items.a: see items
items.why: The first four match their background. The others use armour, spines or a group with many eyes and ears.

items.p: Cows, goats and deer swallow food quickly, then later bring it back up to chew again. This is called chewing the ____.
items.why: Chewing the cud grinds the tough grass finer, so the microbes in the stomach can break it down.

items.p: In the Graze or Hunt race, one rajma bean weighs about as much as 20 rice grains. You pick 30 rice grains and find 2 beans. Which gives you more food?
opts: The 2 beans, which weigh about as much as 40 rice grains
There is no way to tell
items.why: 2 beans weigh about 2 × 20 = 40 grains' worth. 40 is more than 30. Hunters find less often, but each catch is a big meal.

items.p: Draw an antlion's pit from the side. Show where the antlion waits, and how an ant slides in.
items.a: A cone-shaped pit with sloping sides, the antlion buried at the bottom with jaws showing, and an ant slipping down one side.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the steep, loose sides that slide, and the antlion waiting at the very bottom.
items.art: A flat line of sand to draw the pit into.

items.p: A crow eats grain, fruit, insects and leftovers. Why might eating so many kinds of food help crows live in cities?
items.a: In a city there is not much of one kind of food, but there are many kinds. A crow who eats almost anything can always find something.
items.why: A strong answer links eating many foods to finding enough food in a changing place.

items.p: Match each way of hunting to an animal who hunts that way.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each animal gets food in their own way. A strong answer could say one more animal for each way.

items.p: Which of these is NOT camouflage?
opts: A tiger's stripes in dry grass
items.why: The peacock's tail is for showing off, not hiding. The other three match their backgrounds.

items.p: Plan a fair test: does a paper caterpillar hide better on a green dupatta or on a red bedsheet? Say what you would keep the same.
items.a: Use the same green caterpillars on each cloth, the same number and the same size. Hunt for the same time, one strip at a time, with the strips scattered while the hunter's eyes are closed. Do 3 rounds on each. Only the cloth changes.
items.why: A strong plan changes only the background and keeps everything else the same, with more than one round.

worksheets.title: Thinking Like a Hunter, Thinking Like Prey (challenge)

items.p: Deer see fewer colours than we do. Scientists think that to a deer, a tiger's orange may look like green. Explain why this would make a tiger even better hidden in grass.
items.a: If orange looks green to a deer, the tiger's coat matches the green grass. Her black stripes look like the shadows between stems. So to a deer, she blends in even better than she does for us.
items.why: A strong answer sees that camouflage depends on the eyes looking, not only on the body and the place.

items.p: If every tiger caught every deer she chased, what would happen to the deer, and then to the tigers?
items.a: The deer would soon be eaten up. Then the tigers would have nothing to eat, and they would starve too. Tigers need deer to escape most of the time.
items.why: A strong answer follows the chain two steps: fewer deer, then fewer tigers.

items.p: Two sisters in Mysuru argue about a grey moth they found resting on the bark of a tree.

views.says: The moth is just lucky to be that colour. She did not do anything to hide.
The moth chose that tree. Some moths even turn round until their pattern lines up with the bark.

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with? Can both be right? Think about what a moth gets from her parents, and what she might decide for herself.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both can be right. The moth's colour came from her parents and their parents, over many generations. But scientists in South Korea filmed some moths walking and turning on bark until they were better hidden, so where she rests is her choice.
items.why: Colour is passed down. Where and how to rest is decided by the moth. A strong answer separates the two.

items.p: Sunlight comes from above, so the top of a caterpillar is lit and the belly is in shadow. Pastry caterpillars are put on branches for wild birds to find. Which will the birds eat least?
opts: Ones darker on top and paler below
Ones paler on top and darker below
items.why: Darker on top and paler below cancels out the light and shadow, so the caterpillar looks flat and is harder to spot. This is called countershading. When scientists tried this with wild birds, these caterpillars were eaten least.

items.p: A trained hawk attacks two flocks of pigeons, one big and one small. Which flock is more likely to escape?
opts: The big flock, because someone in it notices the hawk sooner
The small flock, because it is quieter
items.why: A real study in England found exactly this. More eyes meant the hawk was noticed sooner, so the big flock took off before she got close.

items.p: A deer who keeps her head down to eat for a long time is easier for a tiger to ambush.
items.why: True. With her head down, a deer cannot see or hear the tiger creeping closer. That is one reason grazers feed in herds, where others keep watch.

items.p: Find the mistake. Someone says, 'Camouflage is a colour. If you paint a strip green, it is camouflaged.' What is wrong with this idea? Use your results from the Paper Caterpillars test.
items.a: Camouflage is a match between a body and a place, not a colour. In my test, the newspaper strips were hidden on the newspaper but easy to see on the plain sheet. A green strip would be hidden on green leaves but not on a white floor.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence that the same strip was hidden in one place and seen in another.

items.p: Invent an animal who lives on your bedroom floor or bedsheet. Draw them with camouflage for that place, and write how they find their food.
items.a: A drawing of an invented animal coloured to match the chosen floor or sheet, with a sentence on how they get food, such as waiting in ambush for crumbs or ants.
items.why: A strong answer matches the colours and pattern of the real place, and gives a way of foraging that fits the animal's body.
items.art: A blank square for the drawing, with lines underneath for writing.

items.p: Sort these hunters: does each one mostly wait for prey, or move after prey?
items: a house gecko by the tube light
a mugger crocodile in a river
a dragonfly catching insects in the air
items.a: see items
items.why: Waiting saves energy but needs prey to come close. Moving after prey costs energy but can find prey anywhere. Dholes and dragonflies chase. The others wait.

items.p: Why do cows swallow grass quickly in the field and chew it properly later?
opts: They can feed fast and chew later, while resting
Their teeth are too weak to chew
Grass tastes better the second time

items.p: A hunt in which the predator waits, still and hidden, then attacks when the prey comes close is called an ____.

applications: Soldiers' uniforms and vehicles use camouflage patterns. Abbott Thayer's ideas helped start this in the First World War.
Wildlife photographers sit in hides and keep still, so animals do not notice them.
Farmers welcome ladybirds, spiders and birds who eat crop pests, instead of using so much poison.
Forest departments count deer and other prey, to know whether a forest can feed its tigers.
Bird feeders with small holes let sparrows and sunbirds eat without bigger birds taking everything.
Fishing nets work like a spider's web: a trap that catches food without chasing it.
Studying how cows and goats graze helps farmers decide how many animals a field can feed.
Scientists copy countershading, and patterns that break up an outline, when they design things that should be hard to see.

open_questions.q: Do prey animals feel fear the way we do?
open_questions.why_open: Their bodies react like ours: hearts race, and they freeze or run. But nobody can feel what another animal feels, so scientists still argue.

open_questions.q: How does a hunter decide when to give up?
open_questions.why_open: Hunters seem to weigh how close they are, how tired they are and whether they have been seen. How they put all this together is not fully known.

open_questions.q: What does the world look like through a deer's eyes, or a bird's?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can test which colours an eye can sense, but not what the animal experiences when they look.

open_questions.q: How many animals hide in ways we cannot see?
open_questions.why_open: Some animals may hide or show patterns in ultraviolet light, or hide their smell. Humans cannot sense these, so many may still be undiscovered.
The first hunters lived in the sea hundreds of millions of years ago and left few traces. Scientists piece the story together from fossils and from living animals such as jellyfish.

open_questions.q: Does a camouflaged moth know that she is hidden?
open_questions.why_open: Some moths turn on bark until they are better hidden. Whether they know they are hidden, or simply settle when the bark feels right under their feet, is not known.

maths.problem: In the Paper Caterpillars test on the newspaper, a hunter caught 15 plain strips and only 3 newspaper strips. How many times as many plain strips did the hunter catch?
maths.explain: The hunter caught 15 plain strips and 3 newspaper strips. 15 divided by 3 is 5. So the hunter caught 5 times as many plain strips. Check: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 15.
maths.why_maths: Saying '5 times as many' tells you how big the difference was. Just saying 'more' does not.
maths.context: This is about the Paper Caterpillars test, where you hunted paper strips on a newspaper for 20 seconds.

maths.problem: In the Still or Moving test, a hunter took 12, 9 and 15 seconds to spot the still strip, and 2, 1 and 3 seconds to spot the wriggling strip. How much longer did the still strip take in all?
maths.explain: Still: 12 + 9 + 15 = 36 seconds. Wriggling: 2 + 1 + 3 = 6 seconds. 36 − 6 = 30. So the still strip took 30 seconds longer to find in all.
maths.why_maths: Adding the three tries together evens out a lucky or unlucky try, so the comparison is fairer.
maths.context: This is about the Still or Moving test, where you timed how long it took to spot a still strip and a wriggling strip.

maths.problem: A herd of 22 chital grazes under a tree with 6 langurs. Each animal has 2 eyes. How many eyes are watching for a tiger? If one chital is alone, how many eyes watch for her?
maths.answer: 56 eyes in the herd and tree. Only 2 for a chital alone.
maths.explain: 22 chital × 2 eyes = 44 eyes. 6 langurs × 2 eyes = 12 eyes. 44 + 12 = 56 eyes. A chital alone has only her own 2 eyes, so the herd has 28 times as many eyes watching.
maths.why_maths: Counting the eyes shows in numbers why living in a group helps prey notice danger sooner.
maths.context: This is about why deer graze in herds. In the story The Bird on the Jeep Track, Arun counted the eyes of the deer in the herd.

maths.problem: In the Graze or Hunt race, one player picked 40 rice grains. Another player found 3 rajma beans. One rajma bean weighs about as much as 20 rice grains. Who collected more food?
maths.answer: The player with the 3 beans, with about 60 grains' worth.
maths.explain: 3 beans × 20 = about 60 rice grains' worth. The other player had 40 grains. 60 is more than 40, so the player with the beans collected more food, even though they picked up far fewer things.
maths.why_maths: Counting pieces alone is misleading. Multiplying by the weight of each piece shows how much food there really was.
maths.context: This is about the Graze or Hunt race, where you picked rice like a grazer and hunted for hidden beans like a hunter.

maths.problem: These are made-up numbers. In one month, a tiger tries 20 hunts and makes 2 kills. How many hunts fail? What fraction of her hunts work?
maths.answer: 18 hunts fail. 2 out of 20 work, which is 1 out of every 10.
maths.explain: 20 − 2 = 18 failed hunts. 2 out of 20 is the same as 1 out of 10, because 20 ÷ 2 = 10. So only 1 hunt in every 10 worked.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows at once how rare success is for a hunter, which is why tigers must try again and again.
maths.context: This is about how often hunters succeed. Real tigers fail in most of their hunts.

roots.context: We have learned how animals find food, and how prey stay alive by watching, keeping still and hiding. Now we ask what hunting and hiding tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Paper Caterpillars test, newspaper strips were hard to find on newspaper but easy to find on plain paper. The strips stayed exactly the same, and only the place under them changed. So hiding is a match between a body and a place. A moth hidden on bark is seen at once on a white wall.
deep_truth.habit: We say an animal 'is camouflaged', as if hiding were a part of their body, like their legs. But the same body is hidden in one place and seen in another. Hiding belongs to the body and the place together, and to the eyes that look.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Paper Caterpillars test, the hunter missed most newspaper strips on the newspaper, then caught most of them on the plain sheet. Nothing about the strips changed. Only the background did.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal who forages too. Like a bird's, your eyes notice what moves and what does not match.
three.what_is_life: Every living being needs food, and most animals must also avoid becoming food. Hunter and hunted each stay alive by noticing the other.
three.what_is_this_world: In this world, how a thing looks depends on where it is and who is looking. A tiger we call orange may look green to a deer.

roots.thread: Sunlight feeds the grass, the grass feeds the chital, and the chital feed the tiger. Over millions of years, the tiger's stripes and quiet paws were shaped by the deer's sharp eyes and ears. The deer's watchfulness was shaped by the tiger. So you cannot explain a tiger without the deer, or a deer without the tiger. The same energy from sunlight passes from the grass to the deer to the tiger, and each animal's body was shaped by the others.

teachings.link: Being hidden is like this. It needs a body, a place and eyes that look, all together. Take away any one of them, and the hiding is gone.

science.text: In experiments with wild birds and paper or pastry prey, prey who matched the background were eaten less often.
What another animal sees and feels when they look at the world can be studied only from outside, by testing their eyes and watching what they do.

other_view.view: A moth's colour came about over many generations, because moths who were easier to see were eaten more often. That explains camouflage fully. It is a fact about bodies, backgrounds and hungry birds, and it carries no message about oneness.

how_we_found_out.story: Abbott Thayer was an American painter who loved birds. In the 1890s he noticed that many animals are darker on their backs and paler on their bellies. He worked out why. Light comes from the sky, so it brightens an animal's back and leaves the belly in shadow. A pale belly evens out that shadow, so the body looks flat and blends into the background. In 1896 he showed this to bird scientists with painted model birds. A model painted dark on top and pale below almost vanished. This is called countershading, and Thayer was right. But then he went too far. In a book he wrote with his son Gerald in 1909, he said that almost every colour on every animal is for hiding. He even said a flamingo's pink hides her against the sky at dawn or dusk. Other naturalists, including Theodore Roosevelt, said this was wrong, because some colours are for showing off or for warning. For about a hundred years, few people tested countershading with real hunters. Then Hannah Rowland and her team in Britain made small pastry caterpillars, coloured in different ways, and laid them on branches. Wild birds ate fewer of the countershaded ones.
how_we_found_out.who: Abbott Thayer, an American painter, with his son Gerald Thayer, and later Hannah Rowland and her team in Britain
how_we_found_out.when: 1896 (the painted model birds), 1909 (the Thayers' book), and the 2000s (the pastry caterpillar tests)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Abbott Thayer believed that almost every animal colour, even a flamingo's pink, is for hiding. Other naturalists showed that some colours are for showing off or warning. His idea of countershading was right, and a century later Hannah Rowland's tests with wild birds and pastry caterpillars showed that it really helps prey survive.
